titleStmt.title: Normalization and variance stabilization of single-cell RNA-seq data using regularized negative binomial regression
titleStmt.author: Christoph Hafemeister
Rahul Satija

publicationStmt.p: Tag layer of the DHSS Meta-Tagging Project. The article text is reproduced from the staged copy named in sourceDesc and is not altered; the tags are held separately in standOff so that overlapping and nested spans are preserved.

bibl.title: Normalization and variance stabilization of single-cell RNA-seq data using regularized negative binomial regression

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: normalisation of single-cell RNA-seq counts - how to remove the effect of sequencing depth without removing the biology along with it
span.quote: The primary goal of single-cell normalization is to remove the influence of technical effects in the underlying molecular counts, while preserving true biological variation.

span.label: whether any single per-cell scaling factor can normalise genes of different abundance, and if not, what error model should replace it
span.quote: These results demonstrate inherent challenges for “size factor”-based normalization strategies. Notably, while recent normalization strategies leverage more advanced strategies to learn cell “size factors”, the use of a single factor will introduce distinct effects on different gene sets, given their average abundance. This suggests that genes may require normalization strategies that depend on their abundance level.

span.label: regularized negative binomial regression - fit a GLM per gene with depth as covariate, pool parameters across genes of similar abundance, and take the Pearson residuals as normalised values
span.quote: We utilize the Pearson residuals (response residuals divided by the expected standard deviation), effectively representing a variance-stabilizing transformation (VST), where both lowly and highly expressed genes are transformed onto a common scale.

span.label: method
span.quote: We utilize the Pearson residuals (response residuals divided by the expected standard deviation), effectively representing a variance-stabilizing transformation (VST), where both lowly and highly expressed genes are transformed onto a common scale.

span.label: a preprocessing choice that decides what counts as biological signal - the same data yielding heterogeneity or not depending on how the error model is constrained
span.quote: To our surprise, we observed significant heterogeneity in the estimates of all three parameters, even for genes with similar average abundance (Fig. 2). These differences could reflect true biological variation in the distribution of single-cell gene expression, but could also represent irreproducible variation driven by overfitting in the regression procedure.

span.label: negative binomial GLM per gene with sequencing depth as covariate, kernel regression to regularize the parameters across genes of similar abundance, and a second constrained fit whose Pearson residuals are the output
span.term: negative binomial GLM per gene with sequencing depth as covariate, kernel regression to regularize the parameters across genes of similar abundance, and a second constrained fit whose Pearson residuals are the output
span.quote: We therefore considered the possibility of constraining the model parameters through regularization, by combining information across similar genes to increase robustness and reduce sampling variation. This approach is commonly applied in learning error models for bulk RNA-seq in the context of differential expression analysis, but to our knowledge has not been previously applied in this context for single-cell normalization.

span.label: counts of low- and high-abundance genes respond differently to sequencing depth, so one factor per cell cannot correct both; dividing by depth leaves the high-abundance tiers still confounded and the variance contribution of the other tiers dampened
span.term: abundance-dependent depth effect defeating a single scaling factor
span.quote: While this approach mitigated the relationship between sequencing depth and gene expression, we found that genes with different overall abundances exhibited distinct patterns after log-normalization, and only low/medium-abundance genes in the bottom three tiers were effectively normalized (Fig. 1d).

span.label: an unconstrained per-gene model has enough freedom to explain real cell-type differences as technical effects of depth, so the residuals it produces have had the biology subtracted along with the noise - even cell-type markers come out with low residual variance
span.quote: When applying standard negative binomial regression, we found that the procedure strikingly removed both technical and biological sources of variation from the data, driven by overfitting of the unconstrained distribution.

span.label: estimating each gene's parameters independently makes them a function of that gene's sampling noise; smoothing them against mean abundance replaces the noise with the population trend, and the estimates become reproducible across bootstraps
span.term: pooling across genes as a constraint
span.quote: We therefore considered the possibility of constraining the model parameters through regularization, by combining information across similar genes to increase robustness and reduce sampling variation. This approach is commonly applied in learning error models for bulk RNA-seq in the context of differential expression analysis, but to our knowledge has not been previously applied in this context for single-cell normalization.

span.label: megakaryocytes carry little RNA, so they appear at low sequencing depth for reasons of biology rather than sampling; an unconstrained fit reads that as a negative slope between depth and the marker's count, which cannot be true of any single cell type
span.term: low RNA content masquerading as a depth relation
span.quote: We observe similar results for the Megakaryocyte (Mk) marker PPBP, but note that both non-regularized models actually fit a negative slope relating total sequencing depth to gene molecule counts. This is because Mk cells have very little RNA content and therefore exhibit lower UMI counts compared to other cell types, even independent of stochastic sampling. However, it is nonsensical to suggest that deeply sequenced Mk cells should contain less PPBP molecules than shallowly sequenced Mk cells, and indeed, regularization of the slope parameter overcomes this problem.

span.label: the regularisation assumes the majority of genes do not vary biologically, which the authors say may be overly simplistic on a highly heterogeneous sample
span.quote: As our workflow leverages all genes (or a random subset) for the initial regularization, we make an implicit assumption that the majority of genes in the dataset do not exhibit significant biological variation. This is analogous to similar assumptions made for bulk RNA-seq normalization and DE (i.e., that the majority of genes are not differentially expressed across conditions).

span.label: the kernel bandwidth is a user-adjustable parameter; robust over an order of magnitude and producing over- or under-smoothing at the extremes
span.quote: Our regularization procedure requires the selection of a kernel bandwidth, which controls the degree of smoothing. We used a data-based bandwidth selection method scaled by a user-defined bandwidth adjustment factor. In Additional file 2: Figure S4, we show that our method returns robust results when varying this parameter within a reasonable range that extends over an order of magnitude, but that extreme values result in over/under-smoothing which will have adverse affects.

span.label: the batch extension requires all cell types to share a similar batch effect, which is an assumption about the experiment rather than a property of the model
span.quote: Finally, while we focus here on modeling technical variation due to differences in cellular sequencing depth, we note that our approach can be easily extended to model alternative “nuisance” parameters, including cell cycle, mitochondrial percentage, or experimental batch, simply by adding additional covariates to the model. Indeed, we observed that a modified GLM including a batch indicator variable was sufficient to correct for technical differences arising from two profiled batches of murine bipolar cells, though successful application requires all cell types to share a similar batch effect (Additional file 2: Figure S8).

span.label: Pearson residuals are an intermediate rather than a model - an alternative would fit the count distribution directly, as GLM-PCA does, instead of passing residuals to methods that assume normal errors
span.quote: Our VST is data driven and does not involve heuristic steps, such as a log-transformation, pseudocount addition, or z-scoring.

span.label: parameter regularisation by pooling across similar features, carried from bulk RNA-seq differential-expression error models into single-cell normalisation
span.quote: We therefore considered the possibility of constraining the model parameters through regularization, by combining information across similar genes to increase robustness and reduce sampling variation. This approach is commonly applied in learning error models for bulk RNA-seq in the context of differential expression analysis, but to our knowledge has not been previously applied in this context for single-cell normalization.

span.label: generalized linear models and Pearson residuals, carried from regression theory to serve as the normalised data values themselves rather than as a diagnostic
span.quote: We utilize the Pearson residuals (response residuals divided by the expected standard deviation), effectively representing a variance-stabilizing transformation (VST), where both lowly and highly expressed genes are transformed onto a common scale.

span.label: a dataset with NO biological variation by construction - droplets that are technical replicates of one bulk RNA sample - run through the unregularised model to see whether the parameter heterogeneity persists when biology cannot explain it
span.note: eliminates: true biological variation as the explanation of the parameter heterogeneity across genes - in a sample where every droplet is a technical replicate of one bulk RNA extract there is no biology left that could produce it · outcome: failed
span.quote: We repeated the same analysis on the “Chromium control dataset,” where the data from each droplet represents a technical replicate of a bulk RNA sample. There is no biological variation in this sample, but parameters from negative binomial regression still exhibited substantial variation across genes, particularly for lowly abundant genes (Additional file 2: Figure S3). Taken together, these results demonstrate that the gene-specific differences we observed were exaggerated due to overfitting.

span.label: the same control dataset run through the FINISHED method, where a correct model must find no high-variance genes at all
span.note: eliminates: residual technical variation as the source of the high-variance genes the finished method selects - run on a sample containing no biology, a correct model must find none, and does · outcome: held
span.quote: We repeated the analysis after subsampling the number of cells in the dataset (Additional file 2: Figure S5) and also on the “Chromium control dataset.” Reassuringly, for the control dataset, we did not observe genes with high residual variance (Additional file 2: Figure S3), demonstrating that our model correctly ascribed all variation in this control dataset to technical sources.

span.label: bootstrapping the fit over randomised subsets of cells, to separate real between-gene differences from sampling variation in the estimates
span.note: eliminates: real between-gene differences as the explanation of the parameter spread - estimates that move when the cells are resampled are measuring the sample and not the gene · outcome: failed
span.quote: To test this, we bootstrapped the analysis by repeatedly fitting a GLM to randomized subsets of cells and assessed the variance of parameter estimates. We found that parameter estimates were not reproducible across bootstraps (Fig. 2), particularly for genes with low to moderate expression levels, and observed highly concordant results when estimating uncertainty using the GLM fisher information matrix as an alternative to bootstrapping (see the “Methods” section and Additional file 2: Figure S2).

span.label: substituting a Poisson and an unconstrained NB error model into the same pipeline, so the regularisation step is tested rather than assumed
span.note: eliminates: the generalised linear model framework itself as the source of the result - swapping only the error model shows the work is done by the regularisation, not by using a GLM · outcome: held
span.quote: When applying standard negative binomial regression, we found that the procedure strikingly removed both technical and biological sources of variation from the data, driven by overfitting of the unconstrained distribution.

span.label: checking what the high-residual-variance genes actually are, rather than reporting that some exist
span.note: eliminates: residual technical noise as the explanation of the surviving high-variance genes - noise does not produce a list that is exclusively markers of known immune cell subsets · outcome: held
span.quote: However, we observed a set of outlier genes with substantially higher residual variance than predicted by our background model, suggesting additional biological sources of variation in addition to sampling noise. Further exploration of these genes revealed that they exclusively represent markers of known immune cell subsets (e.g., PPBP in Megakaryocytes, GNLY in NK cells, IGJ in plasma cells).

span.label: repeating the whole analysis on five UMI datasets from plate- and droplet-based protocols rather than on the one dataset the method was developed against
span.note: eliminates: the single development dataset, and the droplet protocol it came from, as the source of the result · outcome: held
span.quote: We observed identical results when considering any of the five UMI datasets we tested, including both plate- and droplet-based protocols (Additional file 1), demonstrating that our procedure can apply widely to any UMI-based scRNA-seq experiment.

span.quote: The primary goal of single-cell normalization is to remove the influence of technical effects in the underlying molecular counts, while preserving true biological variation.

span.quote: These results demonstrate inherent challenges for “size factor”-based normalization strategies. This suggests that genes may require normalization strategies that depend on their abundance level.

span.label: regularization
span.quote: We therefore considered the possibility of constraining the model parameters through regularization, by combining information across similar genes to increase robustness and reduce sampling variation. This approach is commonly applied in learning error models for bulk RNA-seq in the context of differential expression analysis, but to our knowledge has not been previously applied in this context for single-cell normalization.

span.label: Chromium control dataset
span.quote: We repeated the same analysis on the “Chromium control dataset,” where the data from each droplet represents a technical replicate of a bulk RNA sample. There is no biological variation in this sample, but parameters from negative binomial regression still exhibited substantial variation across genes, particularly for lowly abundant genes (Additional file 2: Figure S3). Taken together, these results demonstrate that the gene-specific differences we observed were exaggerated due to overfitting.

span.label: kernel bandwidth
span.quote: Our regularization procedure requires the selection of a kernel bandwidth, which controls the degree of smoothing. We used a data-based bandwidth selection method scaled by a user-defined bandwidth adjustment factor. In Additional file 2: Figure S4, we show that our method returns robust results when varying this parameter within a reasonable range that extends over an order of magnitude, but that extreme values result in over/under-smoothing which will have adverse affects.

span.label: zero-inflated negative binomial
span.quote: We note that in contrast to our approach, the use of a zero-inflated negative binomial model requires an additional (third) parameter, exacerbating the potential for overfitting. We therefore suggest caution and careful consideration when applying unconstrained NB or ZINB models to scRNA-seq UMI count data.

span.label: Poisson
span.quote: A single-parameter Poisson model performed similarly to our regularized NB, but we observed that residual variances exceeded one for all moderately and highly expressed genes. This is consistent with previous observations in both bulk and single-cell RNA-seq that count data is overdispersed.

span.label: sequencing depth
span.quote: In general, the normalized expression level of a gene should not be correlated with the total sequencing depth of a cell. Downstream analytical tasks (dimensional reduction, differential expression) should also not be influenced by variation in sequencing depth. The variance of a normalized gene (across cells) should primarily reflect biological heterogeneity, independent of gene abundance or sequencing depth. For example, genes with high variance after normalization should be differentially expressed across cell types, while housekeeping genes should exhibit low variance. Additionally, the variance of a gene should be similar when considering either deeply sequenced cells, or shallowly sequenced cells.

span.label: PPBP
span.quote: We observe similar results for the Megakaryocyte (Mk) marker PPBP, but note that both non-regularized models actually fit a negative slope relating total sequencing depth to gene molecule counts. This is because Mk cells have very little RNA content and therefore exhibit lower UMI counts compared to other cell types, even independent of stochastic sampling. However, it is nonsensical to suggest that deeply sequenced Mk cells should contain less PPBP molecules than shallowly sequenced Mk cells, and indeed, regularization of the slope parameter overcomes this problem.

span.label: regularized NB
span.quote: d In contrast to a regularized NB, a Poisson error model does not fully capture the variance in highly expressed genes. An unconstrained (non-regularized) NB model overfits scRNA-seq data, attributing almost all variation to technical effects. As a result, even cell-type markers exhibit low residual variance.

span.label: parameter heterogeneity across genes - READING 1: true biological variation in the distribution of single-cell gene expression
span.quote: To our surprise, we observed significant heterogeneity in the estimates of all three parameters, even for genes with similar average abundance (Fig. 2). These differences could reflect true biological variation in the distribution of single-cell gene expression, but could also represent irreproducible variation driven by overfitting in the regression procedure.

span.label: parameter heterogeneity across genes - READING 2: irreproducible variation driven by overfitting. Resolved in favour of this one by a control dataset with no biological variation in it, where the heterogeneity persisted
span.quote: We repeated the same analysis on the “Chromium control dataset,” where the data from each droplet represents a technical replicate of a bulk RNA sample. There is no biological variation in this sample, but parameters from negative binomial regression still exhibited substantial variation across genes, particularly for lowly abundant genes (Additional file 2: Figure S3). Taken together, these results demonstrate that the gene-specific differences we observed were exaggerated due to overfitting.

span.label: "effectively normalized" - UNDER LOG-NORMALIZATION: true only of the bottom three abundance tiers; high-abundance genes remain confounded with sequencing depth
span.quote: While this approach mitigated the relationship between sequencing depth and gene expression, we found that genes with different overall abundances exhibited distinct patterns after log-normalization, and only low/medium-abundance genes in the bottom three tiers were effectively normalized (Fig. 1d).

span.label: "effectively normalized" - UNDER PEARSON RESIDUALS: level and variance independent of sequencing depth across the full range of expression
span.quote: Our model predicts that for genes with minimal biological heterogeneity in the data (i.e., genes whose variance is driven primarily by differences in sequencing depth), residuals should be distributed with a mean of zero and unit variance. We observe these values for the majority of genes in the dataset (Fig. 4a, b), demonstrating effective and consistent variance stabilization across a range of expression values (Fig. 4c).

span.label: critiques → size-factor normalisation for single-cell data - including recent methods that compute the factor more cleverly, since the problem is the single factor and not its estimation
span.quote: These results demonstrate inherent challenges for “size factor”-based normalization strategies. Notably, while recent normalization strategies leverage more advanced strategies to learn cell “size factors”, the use of a single factor will introduce distinct effects on different gene sets, given their average abundance. This suggests that genes may require normalization strategies that depend on their abundance level.

span.label: critiques → unconstrained negative binomial and zero-inflated negative binomial error models as used in current statistical and deep-learning methods for scRNA-seq
span.quote: Importantly, statistical and deep-learning methods designed for single-cell RNA-seq data often utilize a negative binomial (or zero-inflated negative binomial) error model. Our results suggest that these and future methods could benefit by substituting a regularized model and that including an additional parameter for zero-inflation could exacerbate the risk of overfitting.

span.label: builds-on → regularisation of error-model parameters across genes of similar abundance, standard in bulk RNA-seq differential expression and not previously used for single-cell normalisation

This approach is commonly applied in learning error models for bulk RNA-seq in the context of differential expression analysis, but to our knowledge has not been previously applied in this context for single-cell normalization.

span.quote: To evaluate our regularized NB regression model, we explored the relationship between the Pearson residuals and cellular sequencing depth. Encouragingly, we observed minimal correlation (Fig. 3a, c), for genes across the full range of expression levels. In addition, gene variance was strikingly consistent across cells with different sequencing depths (Fig. 3b, contrast to Fig. 1e), with no evidence of expression “dampening” as we observed when using a cell-level size factor approaches.
